knowledge_point.title: Using the Pythagorean Theorem on the Unit Circle

question.:question/problem: The point $A$ is located in the first quadrant and lies on the unit circle. The $y$-coordinate of $A$ is $\frac{7}{8}$. What is the $x$-coordinate of $A$?
question.:question/worked-solution:
Since the point $A$ lies on the unit circle, it must satisfy the Pythagorean theorem: 

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1
$$

Substituting $y=\frac{7}{8}$ into the above and solving for $x$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+{(\frac{7}{8})}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+(\frac{49}{64}) & =1 \\ {x}^{2} & =1-\frac{49}{64} \\ {x}^{2} & =\frac{15}{64} \\ x & =\sqrt{\frac{15}{64}} \\ x & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{15}}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ lies in the first quadrant, $x$ must be positive, so we select the positive answer. Therefore, our final answer is $x=\frac{\sqrt{15}}{8}.$

knowledge_point.title: Using the Pythagorean Theorem on the Unit Circle

question.:question/problem: The point $A$ is located in the first quadrant and lies on the unit circle. The $y$-coordinate of $A$ is $\frac{3}{5}.$ What is the $x$-coordinate of $A?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Since the point $A$ lies on the unit circle, it must satisfy the Pythagorean theorem: 

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1
$$

Substituting $y=\frac{3}{5}$ into the above and solving for $x$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+{(\frac{3}{5})}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+(\frac{9}{25}) & =1 \\ {x}^{2} & =1-\frac{9}{25} \\ {x}^{2} & =\frac{16}{25} \\ x & =\sqrt{\frac{16}{25}} \\ x & =\pm \frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ lies in the first quadrant, $x$ must be positive, so we select the positive answer. Therefore, our final answer is $x=\frac{4}{5}.$

Since the point $A$ lies on the unit circle, it must satisfy the Pythagorean theorem: 

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1
$$

Substituting $x=\frac{2}{7}$ into the above and solving for $y$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ {(\frac{2}{7})}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ \frac{4}{49}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ {y}^{2} & =1-\frac{4}{49} \\ {y}^{2} & =\frac{45}{49} \\ y & =\sqrt{\frac{45}{49}} \\ y & =\pm \frac{3 \sqrt{5}}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ lies in the first quadrant, $y$ must be positive, so we select the positive answer. Therefore, our final answer is $y=\frac{3 \sqrt{5}}{7}.$

knowledge_point.title: Using the Pythagorean Theorem on the Unit Circle

question.:question/problem: The point $A$ is located in the first quadrant and lies on the unit circle. The $y$-coordinate of $A$ is $\frac{2 \sqrt{3}}{5}.$ What is the $x$-coordinate of $A?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Since the point $A$ lies on the unit circle, it must satisfy the Pythagorean theorem: 

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1
$$

Substituting $y=\frac{2 \sqrt{3}}{5}$ into the above and solving for $x$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+{(\frac{2 \sqrt{3}}{5})}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+(\frac{12}{25}) & =1 \\ {x}^{2} & =1-\frac{12}{25} \\ {x}^{2} & =\frac{13}{25} \\ x & =\sqrt{\frac{13}{25}} \\ x & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{13}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ lies in the first quadrant, $x$ must be positive, so we select the positive answer. Therefore, our final answer is $x=\frac{\sqrt{13}}{5}.$

knowledge_point.title: Using the Pythagorean Theorem on the Unit Circle

question.:question/problem: The point $A$ is located in the first quadrant and lies on the unit circle. The $y$-coordinate of $A$ is $\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}.$ What is the $x$-coordinate of $A?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Since the point $A$ lies on the unit circle, it must satisfy the Pythagorean theorem: 

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1
$$

Substituting $y=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}$ into the above and solving for $x$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+{(\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5})}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+(\frac{1}{5}) & =1 \\ {x}^{2} & =1-\frac{1}{5} \\ {x}^{2} & =\frac{4}{5} \\ x & =\sqrt{\frac{4}{5}} \\ x & =\pm \frac{2 \sqrt{5}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ lies in the first quadrant, $x$ must be positive, so we select the positive answer. Therefore, our final answer is $x=\frac{2 \sqrt{5}}{5}.$

knowledge_point.title: Using the Pythagorean Theorem on the Unit Circle

question.:question/problem: The point $A$ is located in the first quadrant and lies on the unit circle. The $x$-coordinate of $A$ is $\frac{\sqrt{11}}{7}.$ What is the $y$-coordinate of $A?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Since the point $A$ lies on the unit circle, it must satisfy the Pythagorean theorem: 

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1
$$

Substituting $x=\frac{\sqrt{11}}{7}$ into the above and solving for $y$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ {(\frac{\sqrt{11}}{7})}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ \frac{11}{49}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ {y}^{2} & =1-\frac{11}{49} \\ {y}^{2} & =\frac{38}{49} \\ y & =\sqrt{\frac{38}{49}} \\ y & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{38}}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ lies in the first quadrant, $y$ must be positive, so we select the positive answer. Therefore, our final answer is $y=\frac{\sqrt{38}}{7}.$

knowledge_point.title: Using the Pythagorean Theorem on the Unit Circle

question.:question/problem: The point $A$ is located in the first quadrant and lies on the unit circle. The $y$-coordinate of $A$ is $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.$ What is the $x$-coordinate of $A?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Since the point $A$ lies on the unit circle, it must satisfy the Pythagorean theorem: 

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1
$$

Substituting $y=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ into the above and solving for $x$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+(\frac{1}{2}) & =1 \\ {x}^{2} & =1-\frac{1}{2} \\ {x}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ x & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}} \\ x & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ lies in the first quadrant, $x$ must be positive, so we select the positive answer. Therefore, our final answer is $x=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.$

knowledge_point.title: Using the Pythagorean Theorem on the Unit Circle

question.:question/problem: The point $A$ is located in the first quadrant and lies on the unit circle. The $x$-coordinate of $A$ is $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{7}.$ What is the $y$-coordinate of $A?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Since the point $A$ lies on the unit circle, it must satisfy the Pythagorean theorem: 

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1
$$

Substituting $x=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{7}$ into the above and solving for $y$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ {(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{7})}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ \frac{3}{49}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ {y}^{2} & =1-\frac{3}{49} \\ {y}^{2} & =\frac{46}{49} \\ y & =\sqrt{\frac{46}{49}} \\ y & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{46}}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ lies in the first quadrant, $y$ must be positive, so we select the positive answer. Therefore, our final answer is $y=\frac{\sqrt{46}}{7}.$

question.:question/problem: The point $A$ is located in the first quadrant and lies on the unit circle. The $y$-coordinate of $A$ is $\frac{3}{4}.$ What is the $x$-coordinate of $A?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Since the point $A$ lies on the unit circle, it must satisfy the Pythagorean theorem: 

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1
$$

Substituting $y=\frac{3}{4}$ into the above and solving for $x$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+{(\frac{3}{4})}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+(\frac{9}{16}) & =1 \\ {x}^{2} & =1-\frac{9}{16} \\ {x}^{2} & =\frac{7}{16} \\ x & =\sqrt{\frac{7}{16}} \\ x & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{7}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ lies in the first quadrant, $x$ must be positive, so we select the positive answer. Therefore, our final answer is $x=\frac{\sqrt{7}}{4}.$
